blocks.x: And my brother too did.
They made a moving picture of the big Jack, the big... Yeah, my brother was coming out today.
Made a picture of Black Benny. Made a picture of his funeral.
I never heard about it.
No. Me and Ray and Happy was grand march. The funeral was seven blocks long. Long for a nickel insurance.
A nickel insurance?
Long for a nickel insurance. Had to put a sauce on his stuff and beg the better. And he had one of the greatest years in the office.
You had to do what?
Had to put a sauce on his chest and beg him under the better.
Oh.

So I mean the Zulu Club they turned out too. The Zulu Club turned out, they turned out too. When me and Black Benny was... I mean me and Ray and Happy, they was the grand march. And they'd never forget that.
Somebody told me they had this drum up on top of the hearse or someplace. Do you remember? Is that true? No.
I didn't remember it had this drum on the hearse.
They had flowers all around it. Maybe on top of the casket or someplace. I don't know.
Well, they had plenty of flowers. They had plenty of flowers.
But they had the drum up there too. Do you remember that?

Well, I remember about the drum being up there. I remember that. But I remember having one of the greatest funerals. It was seven blocks long and the greatest second line. You know, he'd come out from Cadillus Street, you know. And Marty was slippers were sliding. It was a horrible thing. Yeah, they made a picture. They just like they made a picture of my brother's funeral when it was coming out. They took the picture of us when he was coming out the house and right at this church here, Catholic Church Tulane. Right across the street from the house, Bill. And Catron made a picture of that. Now, you all want to go way back to Jordan Bay Shearing with a little bit of boys. Is that what you want?
Well, first we'd like to get your name down here. All right.
Joseph Rennie.
And your name?
Marjorie Zander. Paul Crawford. Bill Russell.
And Dick Allen. Is that the middle name? No, it's Joseph Rennie. That's all. We just always carried two names. They had a middle one. We wouldn't know nothing about it.
How do you spell Rennie really?

Well, we used to, when we was playing music, we used to put an R-E-N-E. But now I go on to the R-E-N-E. R-E-N-E, R-E-N-E-A. The name, see? Well, the E have the sound of A, but now I use E now instead of A. But the time we used to play, we used the A.

So your original name is with two E's. Yeah, two E's. R-E-N-E-A. Let's see now. We're about to get the date on here too. Today is Thursday, April? The 7th. The 7th in 1960. And we were recording this at the Kingdom Hall. Yeah, that's right. It's the Seventh-day Adventist Church Hall. No Jehovah's Witnesses. Oh, Jehovah's Witnesses. What am I thinking about?
I read the wrong thing. Yeah.
I'm staring at the 7th.
Huh?
Today being the 7th.
Today being the 7th. Well, you had that on your mind. That's why we're having it tomorrow. Yeah.
Jehovah's Witnesses. And you're now a minister. Minister, yeah.

I've been a minister since 39. When I was old, Danny, in 39. I see. And I retired in music in the 1942's when I retired. From John Dennis Alvin Station. And that was from the Budweiser Dance Hall when I retired. Oh, yeah. Yeah. All those jobs, they were just...
Who else was working with you there?
Well, we had a brother, a fellow by the name, Sport Young. Oh, yeah.
Austin Young.
Austin Young and his brother. They played the trambone. Saxophone. Or the sport saxophone. Yeah, well he had a brother who played the trambone too.
I heard Austin there in 1942 too.

Austin, yeah, yeah. And then Handy. What was he playing? Bass. His brother was playing bass. Eddie Hand, no Eddie Hand is the saxophone player. You see John Handy is the bass player. John Handy is the bass player, yeah.
No, John Handy played saxophone and clarinet. Yeah, that's right. And the bass player, Sylvester.

But he played a while there with us. And also Duke Deconje played the piano. And Butler rap. Gaillet. Gaillet, yeah. He played the guitar. And I played the drum. Duke Deconje? Duke Deconje, yeah. He played the piano with us. Does he play any other instruments? No, he just played none of the piano. He got killed. You know he had a shoe shop there on Ramport near Common and he went out with this this fellow played the piano, Richardson they called him. Herbert Richardson, you know Herbert Richardson? No? Well he went out one time to get some shoe business and he had a little food and he got in a wreck. He got killed. Now that's why we just used this fellow they called Walter Decon when I was the last one. So we had a little scrummage up there, you see. And after the scrummage let's see who we got to play the piano. Let's see if I can think who we had to play the piano.
He must have had a different guitar player too after that. Yeah we did.
Well I don't know about the place since this opened so long after that I think.
Did Johnny Cicero ever play with you there?
No, Johnny Cicero played spot jobs.
I heard him there one time too about 1942. I wondered if he took.

I think they must have took over because I know they left me after the scrummage. Yeah, yeah, yeah. In 42 that's the time they must have took over. Oh yeah this other little boy Papadie called him. He went back there. They had another section because after that scrummage happened I don't know.
What did Papadie play?
Drummer.
You never did know his real name? Foster, I do.
Foster?
Foster, that's his name. Is he any relation to Earl Foster? No, no, no relative at all. Just Papad Foster? No, it's not a. Not Chy B.
Oh no, not a lot.
You talk White Bear.
I saw a little dick named White Bear. He hangs in a burglar's spread out of the hood. Him and this fellow Deku. That's where they hang out. Every night if I want to find him to look him up.
Well they, let's see, Deku was living with the two of them. I was there with Tom Alba, you know. Tom Alba still got that place. Oh, down Burgundy Street?
Down Burgundy Street.
Yeah, yeah.
Is he still living yet?
Oh sure. I see him once a week or so, maybe twice. Oh yeah. I'm always passing by. Oh yeah, I see.
I believe he's 82 now, about that age.
Yeah, he's pretty old man.
In the 83 even.
He's a pretty old man, because he was, when I was a young man, he was pretty good up in the age. He must have been around a man about 35, 40 years at that time. I mean I'm 63 now. I'll be 63.
Well we were going to ask, what is your birthday?
First day of March, 1897. March the first, 1897. Were you born right here in New Orleans?
Born in New Orleans.
What section? The Creole section. What we call the Trimmy.
What about your brother, was he old or young?

No, he was the youngest one. He was young like me. I've got plenty to tell you now, I'll tell you. Well. I'll tell you now, you might want to know a history about Beyshe, or who you want to know about. Let me tell you, just tell me.
Anybody, anybody you want to talk about. We'd like to know about you first. Well. And your family, you know. Anybody else in your family played, other than your brother, and you?

Well my daddy, my daddy was, he was a born musician. He used to work for Roy Lyre years ago. I understand he was the first man to put the foil in the ghetto. That's what I understand. He played ghetto, in other words he played all string instruments. Then he could repair stringing. He could make manly the ghettos. He was that way. He was a pretty good musician. That's all I can tell you about him.
Did your mother play anything?

My mother used to play the ghetto. I remember she used to play the ghetto and she used to sing. Well that's the time they began to cook them. The girl called it cow and it's turtle. But these, you know, when they get full of their little wine and turtles, they'd sit down. We'd play the band and she'd play the ghetto. And we'd sit out on the floor and sing, you know what I mean, until we'd get to sleep. And that was it. That's all I remember that.
Did he play jazz, what you call ragtime? Or was he strictly a reader or what?
No, I don't think he was a reader. I just think he just, this ability, this man just had that in here. According to what, I tell you a fella that kind of know him, but you know Slowdrag?
Oh yeah.

Well he used to, my daddy was, he used to come to be in what they call a wine head. And he used to bum on Espe, on the domain in Viro, and he used to call it Boss. But I mean a lot of them old heads, they're gone. But Slowdrag knows something about my daddy, by the name of Boss. Well that's the place he used to hang out every day. A better fella fell right in his footsteps. Samway hanging in the bottom, just like that. And he took the harvest, you know, and he died. Another foe, another word, he died from an elixir police hit him, you know. Never forget that boy, he was running. He was running me about 15 or 20 blocks, maybe more than that. He was running me for about a half hour. And he was saying, Blue, he's calling me the devil. He's calling my brother Angel. I'm my brother Drake just like you. He called me Angel. And he's calling me Blue, Blue, catch that devil man. And I know about to be the soul as well. That's right. But I tell you though, most of all the boys, I'll tell you, there ain't nobody ever that played Caravan like I did. Caravan. Man, I had a triple solo on that thing. It was just as nice and smooth, and a tom-tom and a rack, see. One of them gong racks. Then I had another tom-tom and I was making triplets. And I played that solo and it just, it was a beautiful. Let's see. Let's see if I... I just can't get that rhythm again, you know what I mean? But everybody said I really played that.
What kind of a drum set did you have? How big was your band?

I had a little, oh, at them times, 32 inches. 32 to 14 wide. Oh yeah, they believed in bass drum and they believed in kicking them through the instrument. See that's the way we used to play drums sometimes. When they had them swinging pedals, the leader pedals, you all remember them swinging pedals?
I've seen them I played.

Well then the bass drum, you could actually, if the wind was blowing this way, and it would be at night when things were solid or solid, you could actually hear my bass drum at least a mile. Well I'll tell you to prove that fact, we used to play at the Bulls Club. And they said, yeah, my brother, that's on eighth and round, and Daniel they call it. Well they shoot them down on Canal and Claiborne. That's right.
The bass drum and the trumpet.
Just kick it wide open, see?
You'd have your foot up off the floor when you hit the bass drum. Yeah, just like that, kick it in the thick like that. Just hitting it with your toe, huh?
Just riding them swinging pedals, see? We got our foot flat after we got there, love with you, swinging pedals, I mean them down pedals.
You used to move your whole leg from your hip joint pedals.
That's right.
What kind of snare drum did you have?
Well I had a 14 by 15, I mean a 6 by 14.
And a metal, metal, metal, yeah.
And a corner hook and a flesh hook was wood.
What kind of make, do you remember the make?
Oh yeah, I used to like a leader. Yeah, I liked the leader drum.
How many cymbals did you use?

I used one crash cymbal. Chinese? Chinese crash cymbal. And hit it wide open. Oh man, the drummer was a noisy thing. And the people liked that noise, you know? And another thing too, again, in the days like that, it looked like the lollier play, a lot of people like it. Like that Mr. Clot Miller, buddy, you know? Y'all heard of Blind Gilbert? Oh yeah, I know him. You used to work with him? Eh? No, no, I didn't work with him, but one time we, you see when they draw the crowd, they had my brother and Louis Armstrong. They was playing together. And they hired the people just to draw a crowd. They had a crowd on both of them. And you know old God was to play some trumpets, you know? Oh boy, I'll tell you. Now Louis, I, well let's see, you want to know about me first after this, because I've got so much to tell you. Oh, we know.
Yeah, I was gonna ask you.
Because I think I'm by the honest one who knew anything about everything, you know? You know, because I got to.
You can ask more about the drum set, however, on it.
Oh yeah, yeah, drum set. It was the leaded.
These tom-toms, these tom-toms, what kind of.
Well, you know them sort of a Chinese tom-toms with a dragon on it?
With all the little nails on it.
And then, yeah, then they had another black tom-toms, sort of a black tom-toms. Big deep one. Yeah, yeah, about six years, and it sat on the stand. Oh yeah, they had a nice sound.
Did you use any other tracks like cowbells or?
No, I didn't lose beaters in love with. Woodblock ever? Woodblock, oh yeah, woodblock, four cowbells.
Did you ever play on the rims on the air? Oh yeah, all that, chill, all that chill. We used to play all that.

We'd get over, you see, when we'd get to playing waltzes and things like that, you might could hear some of them on that record. I had some of the off his beat, I don't know if it was, well, I had some off beats that could almost throw a man off, you see, but we were just used to that, you know, after effect, you see. And while my brother could play so good, I was considered as a man, held time like a cloud. Do you know I was the honest drummer? A fellow was talking about that down the day. You know the boy who played the trombone I was talking with when he was there on the Jackson Avenue by that church there?
I see, that was the young shell boy.

Yeah, yeah, well he can tell you, I was the honest man who never played a drum sleeping. I was solid, I was snowing. I was the honest man who played drums, then he slept for two hours. I was like, I'm a little bit of a drum, I never break that drum, I changed that time. See, I never changed that time. That's right, if they changed the walls, I stayed with the fox rod, I just changed like that, just changed like that, sleeping for two, three hours. And you hear me tell you, because them fellows used to come watch me. And I'd be snowing, they'd know I was sleeping. So that's what they're fighting for sleeping. I was a walking, sleeping drummer.
Somebody else I heard used to go to sleep playing drums, I can't think of.
Johnny Sincere used to go to sleep playing guitar, I remember. Yeah. I wanted to ask you about tuning your drums, you told me about that the other day.

Oh yeah, yeah. Well now, I used to tune my drum in G, with the G string on the bass. That's the bass drum? That's the bass drum. It'd get a beautiful sound. And then you can tune with either one of them strings, it'd depend, you know. Now sometimes I used to tune my drum, like a lot of times we used to play a lot of stuff in G and D, you know, in A and stuff like that. And when we'd get numbers in different key like that, then I'd tune my drum in the- You know, I got that idea, I got that idea from the Tiffany. I used to go out to Palace Theater a lot, a lot of musicians, that's the way they used to do in the morning time, you know, in the evening. They'd go to Palace Theater, and they had that fellow, I forgot his name, but that was a wonderful drummer, one of the best white drummers I ever heard in my son. I'd be there calling him Stein about me. He was a wonderful drummer. He was glad to say, you see what the name of the violin player already. I think that man's still living, he left downtown there. But he was one of the best drummers, and he used everything that comes to the drum.
Emil Tasso, would that be?

Yeah, that's Tasso's right. He was the leader of that man. But that was a wonderful drummer, he was the leader. Ace man. And he had timpani, and bells, and chimes, he had everything. And, well I was pretty, a fellow would always, it sounds something, and the bass drum had a beautiful sound. So I'd carry it. Right now, in my grip, I got all my music paper, you know, doing my trance, you know, arranging. I've got, still got a guitar tuner. That's how I catch things, you know. And you know what I used to do sometimes, we would catch fellas. I'd stand out and write what they make. But I never was a flashy drummer. I was a drummer, I always didn't believe in support. That's one of the main things. When a drummer, you see Johnny, Johnny was a drummer, he played, he played a nice drummer. He used to throw the band off a lot of the time. See, you want to be flashy, making all of them explosions, you see. But I never was that. I was a drummer, always keep a smooth, smooth time. And I always kept, I was supporting my brother. I was supporting the band, you see. I wasn't trying to, you know, make a name for myself. I was pushing in. And he could do anything he wanted on that trumpet. Now I'm going to tell you all some secret after a while. Do you even mind me behind those? I used to always fool the planet, I got to play in that shit. The mouthpieces used to be round, see. And I used to make high notes. I started them off making high notes. And Louis would chop it behind my brother. We used to take the mouthpiece and go and paint them, flatten them. But today they got a different system. They got a secret now they got now, what they call, non-pressure. But at the time them fellas had to catch a good bit in that mouthpiece. They'd flatten that mouthpiece. I had to flatten that mouthpiece and cut that cup. That's how they called Louis-Ange-Ange-Ange Dipper. That way they got their stuff from Dipper, you see. Where they fix to the cup. The mouthpiece be deep, you know. It'll just like Dipper. And they'll just round them off and then they'll take them. Moved sandpaper and shoot. And by their little get in there and stay like that. They had to get anything they want. No, they used a stone.
Oh right on the stone.

You lose an emery stone, you see. Grind it down fine, fine. Then you get a fine, fine sandpaper, you see. Then you get an oil stone to finish it all. But you get that cup flat, you see. Lift it straight and you see. And when you get in there, man, hook up in there and stay there. Make it what you want. That was my brother's secret.
I think now they make them shallow.

Oh yeah, they're making it. Well, they started, I'll tell you why they started making them shallow. I remember several fellas come paper writers, you know, they asked me to look at his home, they asked him his mouthpiece, and they asked him, why did he get a mouthpiece flat like that? I remember that, but I can't remember the writer. I know one fella from New York, a paper writer, and he wanted to know, why can you buy a mouthpiece? You can't buy a mouthpiece like that. Well, you see, they can get anything they want out of my brother. Come give him flasks of whiskey, man, that's all. He's just like a food dog, you tie a chair out. He gone, he followed that drink, you see. And they just went and told the man what it was, you see. And we spiked his back in the yard, you know, and I used to make the high notes on the clarinets, you know, and he tried to catch me. And he'd go back there and fire again till he'd catch that grip. And that was it. He was the first one around him to start to make high notes.
And I tell you,

of course, they didn't want to give me the credit. I didn't want it, no, huh? Because all I was trying to do, take the ideas, you know, to get ahead of the other fella. I went to the, this must have been back in 1910 or 11, but way back then, got a coconut shell and cut it in half. Because you see, I've seen Buddy Petit, but the first one played, you know, with his derby. He was the first man ever played with a derby, you see, and him and another fella, Frederick Kepage, you all heard talking about Frederick Kepage, yeah. But I know all them fellas, man, you praise and all them. Well then, he was the first one used to play with his derby, you see. But now when he took his derby off, I heard him say, wow, just like that. So I told my brother I had caught something. I hadn't caught a knife, you know. So he said, I said, I said, Buddy Petit there, made something out of it. He said, well, Trump had said, wow, just like that. So, he figured out, he figured out, I said, well, I wonder how he did. I said, well, he took his derby. He said, my brother, took a guy to the derby, you see, when he went to playing, and, well, he went to fanning, you see, and he kept saying, wow, wow. I said, it was all right, but man, the derby got broke and he had nothing else. He tried to use his hand then, you see. So I studied, I said, well, you see, at that time, I used to play in a little show one time to make the horse hoof, you know, I cut the coconut shell. So he said, try that coconut shell, and he began to cut it in the show. So that coconut shell, I said, I don't know about a yellow, so after he had come to the wild, I'm reading it. So now, Chris Kelly, he got an idea. He stuck a, you, you ain't think so, boy, one of them, one of them flushes,
Charlie Flushes,

and he began to play, wow, wow, we began to play the blues with that. Them fellas used to figure all kinds of items, that's how we used to do, try to out scheme one another, you know. But my brother, he just had a good tone in the horn, and he played clean, and I played nice, straight drums. And that's, in other words, I'd consider my style as a standard style, because the time and the swing, I had the time and I had the swing, you see, and that's good. And that's the thing, I think, you'll always stay in a nice, a nice, what we call a nice jazz music rhythm, sort of a trumpet player, playing sort of a straight, nice melody, but always put nice little, not too much, you see. Now, I ain't talking about this rock and roll, because that stuff ain't nothing. Because you can play D&G, that's all you get, you see. But the time we had to play, you had to just, like right now, seven augmentation, the diminished chords and all that. That's what made all them fellas, like bitch, ain't such a good plan to play. Them fellas had all that up in their head, you see. Except now rock and roll, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do, do. Da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da, da. Do, do, do, do, do, do. See what I mean? Only two, three chords. That's a rhythm. That's all. This ain't gonna last long. Rock and roll ain't gonna last long. But jazz will always stand. Jazz with a nice, smooth rhythm. Don't you think so? What y'all think? It's a nice style dance of music, you know? It's a nice style. It's actually a nice style dance of music. It's gonna stand.
How high could your brother go?

How high could your brother go? Well, the fellas say he made F on the trumpet, above the staff. F. One day he made F. When they didn't drink that night, he was feeling good. He'd come out there and he made F. And E and all that stuff. He used to go so much, it almost sounded like a whistle. But the tone was clad the crystal, he'd make it clad. And I'll tell you how they know that. You see the fellas just take them on the clarinet. The fella called Zeb, you know, he was playing with us then. And he used to make that note on his clarinet, he said, man he made F.
What was Zeb's last name? Do you know?
Let me see. Zeb Linares, I think it was. Zeb Linares. He was living there on Tala Don Street.
He was on Tala Don. I think that's where he was living at. Yeah.
Do you know when he died? How long ago?

Well no, he died, let's see where he was at, the last time he came in. Because he was in the Tennessee hospital, veteran hospital, you know. And they told him not to drink so he came in and went to drink. And I can't remember them, see I can't remember them years. But I can remember these activities, you know. Was it before?
Was it before? Did he die before your brother or after?
Oh no, he died before my brother. Oh before?
Was that before World War II or after? Or during?

Oh no, I think that Zeb died there. I think he died after World War II. That's the time I think he died. You remember I say that because we were playing somewhere and my brother was playing and he came and visited us, you see. I don't know, somebody started him off with drinking.
It was before 1942 then probably. I think somewhere around there.
You were still playing when he died? Who? When Zeb died you were still playing?
Oh yeah, I just was on in 42. Yeah so. Yeah, it was the Budweiser dance hall. I'll never forget that in 42.
Where was that show you played where you used the horse's grill?

Well that's used to call it Miro Show. A fella by the name of Anor, a little short Creole fella, he used to have a show back there. He used to run the picture then after the dance. That's an old show back on Miro with the Anzaga and Dabba Dee, something like that. The whole time. The moving pictures then? Yeah, he used to have moving pictures and after you run the picture then after the dance. We played at two o'clock. Running pictures about an hour. See I used to imitate. They didn't have no talking pictures then. See a drummer had to imitate everything. Oh man I had Slave Bell, I had Duck Whistle, Cow, Crow Caller. Oh I had a piece of my, almost as big as this. My drummer had a load. And then you, no drummer wouldn't want a little drum. They laugh at you that drum. 32 by 14.
Did you ever use the hi-hat or sock cymbal? The one with your left? Yeah, yeah I used the sock cymbal, yeah.

And I tell you what, I started using the sock cymbal, started using the sock cymbal at the Budweiser Dan Hall. That was around in 35 when I started using the sock cymbal. I didn't have no sock cymbal when I went there, but I bought one after and I began to use it.
We were wondering, when you first started in music, did you have any lessons? Did you say guitar was your first instrument or how did you get started?

No, no, but you see my brother was locked up in the waveform. You know, talking about Jones. That was Lewis and that boy. They had a little band. Lewis Armstrong had a little band and a man by the name of Dave, he's still living here. They call him Professor Dave. And they used to go back there and lesson. Well I was trying to play the clan that day, you see. And me and a fella by the name of Jimmer Brown and another dog fella played trumpet. Well let's see what his name is. He died there too recently a few years back. Big dog fella. He used to go back there and take lessons. Where did he live? He lived somewhere around Cadena Street.
Did you have another, well there's one guy named Shots back there.

Yeah that's who I'm talking about, Shots. That's who I'm talking about, Shots. Yeah, Shots used to go back there. Well I was trying to fool with clan that then. Now you're coming back, now you're talking about the tailgate. Tailgate time man, one of the bass and the tram owners sitting back on the tailgate. We used to use the furniture wagons. When I first started though they had horses. They used no truck. They used horses because we used to advertise for show down here on N-H street. And they started there, we used to have horses at that time. Then after I began to work for Beans and Rick and Ford and them at the Astro, they called it Tik Tok. We used to advertise the truck. There used to be some time then. The fellas would get there and chain them truck together. Sit right there and that was my...
Where did you have the drums on the wagon?
In the back, in the front. Way in the drum.
Where the drums were riding?

Yeah, nice of the driver. That's where the drummer was sitting. Yeah. And the bass and the trombone was sitting right on the tailgate. They were, the bass had these bass on them. And then the trombone had to be tailgate, two slides on. Ghetto and clarinet, trumpet all in the inside. It was so tiny. Now, what else y'all want to know?
When you started, did you have any feature on clarinet or pick it up yourself?

I picked it up myself. I picked it up myself. I picked it up myself. Now on drum, I picked it up myself, but there's a fellow by the name of Floyd Casey. He came down here with no Faith Marvelous, with Faith Marvel. It was him and Floyd Casey and he was a wonderful drummer too.
That's the same guy who used to work with Dewey Jackson? Might have been.

I know he's from way around St. Louis. Yeah, well they played on St. Louis. Yeah, he had a four octave I think of Viperphone. No, he wasn't a Viperphone, remember. Yeah. And then he could play piano too. He was a wonderful drummer. Well I took some lessons for him. But see, after he, I was a fellow to advance fast. I took lessons on the clarinet too, but a fellow wanted to take me away from him because I, I used to, that sit out, you see the method to make the clarinet now, is very simplified. You notice all the youngsters in the school now holding the clarinet down? Oh man, it's beautiful. She's supposed to hold the clarinet on a 45 degree. Some of them hold them, some of them jump on that. For all the schools, all the professors want the money, they ain't giving the real heart of holding the clarinet. And that's important. See, because some of them have some good tones, and I put a nice tone to the clarinet. But I always got that idea from Bechet and them fellas, you know. Well tell us about Sidney Bechet. Yeah, now Sidney Bechet, now let me tell you about that. He used to play a flute, what they call a fife. And my brother had a comb and some of this old brown, thin brown paper. And I went around the market and I got, you know cheese bars, some old cheese bars? Well I went and got some meat off the round steak, that skin, and made drums. segments.title: Black Benny's funeral and the grand march
segments.summary: Rene recalls the long funeral of Black Benny, filmed, with himself, Ray and Happy leading the grand march and the Zulu Club turning out; Zander asks about a drum on the hearse.

segments.chapter: Opening and the Budweiser Dance Hall
segments.title: Opening: names, spelling of Rene, date and place of recording
segments.summary: Names of those present are recorded, Rene explains his surname spelling, and the date (7 April 1960) and Kingdom Hall location are set; he notes he is a minister.

segments.chapter: Opening and the Budweiser Dance Hall
segments.title: Retiring from music in 1942: the Budweiser Dance Hall band
segments.summary: Rene says he became a minister in 1939 and retired from music in 1942 from the Budweiser Dance Hall, naming Austin Young, Handy, Duke Deconje on piano and a guitarist, and how the pianist was killed.

segments.chapter: Opening and the Budweiser Dance Hall
segments.title: Who took over after the 1942 break-up, and Papadie the drummer
segments.summary: Zander asks about Johnny Cicero; Rene says others took over after the trouble in 1942, and Russell identifies the drummer Papadie as surnamed Foster.

segments.title: White Bear, Deku and the old trumpeter living on Burgundy Street
segments.summary: Talk of local musicians' hangouts and an elderly man still living on Burgundy Street whom Rene knew when he was young.

segments.title: Birth date and birthplace in the Creole Treme section
segments.summary: Rene was born 1 March 1897 in New Orleans in the Creole section and says his brother was the youngest like him.

segments.title: His musician father Boss and his mother who played guitar
segments.summary: Rene describes his father as a born string player and repairer and his mother playing guitar and singing; Slow Drag knew his father, called Boss, and Rene recalls a childhood chase. He also boasts of his triple tom-tom solo on Caravan.

segments.title: Bass drum size, swinging pedals and foot technique
segments.summary: He describes his 32-inch bass drum, its carrying power, and how the swinging pedals were played with the leg kicking wide open.

segments.title: Rene's drum set: snare, cymbal, tom-toms and traps
segments.summary: Zander asks about snare, make, crash cymbal, Chinese tom-toms, woodblock and cowbells; Rene mentions his brother and Louis Armstrong drawing a crowd.

segments.title: Keeping steady time: the sleeping drummer
segments.summary: Rene says he held time solidly and could play for hours asleep, and Russell mentions another musician who slept while playing.

segments.title: Tuning the drums and the Palace Theater drummer
segments.summary: He tuned the bass drum to the guitar string, learning from a Palace Theater drummer identified as Emil Tasso, and says he was never a flashy drummer but supported his brother.

segments.chapter: Brother's trumpet and the early players
segments.title: His brother's flattened trumpet mouthpiece secret
segments.summary: Rene describes how his brother flattened the mouthpiece cup with emery stone and sandpaper to play high notes, and why writers asked about it.

segments.chapter: Brother's trumpet and the early players
segments.title: Mutes: coconut shell, derby and plunger, and rock and roll
segments.summary: Rene tells how mute ideas came from Buddy Petit's derby, a coconut shell and a plunger used by Chris Kelly, and ends by arguing jazz will outlast rock and roll.

segments.chapter: Brother's trumpet and the early players
segments.title: How high his brother could play and Zeb Linares
segments.summary: His brother reached high F, confirmed by clarinetist Zeb Linares, whose death is placed around 1942.

segments.title: Accompanying silent films at the Miro show and the sock cymbal
segments.summary: Rene played traps and sound effects for silent pictures and dances at a show on Miro, and started using the sock cymbal at the Budweiser around 1935.

segments.title: First instruments and early lessons
segments.summary: Rene says the early teacher Professor Dave taught Armstrong and others, and he and Shots took lessons.

segments.title: Advertising on wagons and trucks: where the band sat
segments.summary: He describes tailgate advertising from horse-drawn wagons to trucks and where the drummer, bass and trombone sat.

segments.title: Teaching himself, Floyd Casey's lessons and a homemade first band
segments.summary: He taught himself clarinet and drums, took lessons from drummer Floyd Casey, and recalls making homemade drums with his brother.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet playing for beer; spelling of Rishack
segments.summary: Rene recounts Bechet getting a clarinet as a Christmas gift and playing in clubs for cans of beer; Zander asks how the venue name Rishack is spelled.
